title: Manager Updates
description: Concise status, risk callouts, and decision requests.

items.scenario: Your manager asks for a weekly status on the reliability roadmap. Two initiatives are on track; one is blocked on security review.
items.prompt: What is the strongest opening status line?

choices.text: Busy week, lots of meetings.
Two of three reliability initiatives are on track. The SLO dashboard work is blocked on security review; I need your help unblocking by Friday or we slip the release by one sprint.
Everything is fine unless something changes.
I will send a long document later.

items.explanation: Managers need progress, blockers, and a clear ask with a deadline impact.

items.scenario: You discovered a capacity risk: current traffic growth will exhaust DB CPU in about six weeks if unchanged.
items.prompt: How do you escalate the risk?

choices.text: The database might get slow someday.

Risk: at current growth, DB CPU hits saturation in ~6 weeks. Impact: elevated latency and possible checkout errors. Options: (1) scale vertically this month, (2) accelerate read-replica work. I recommend option 1 as a bridge; need budget approval by next Tuesday.
We should panic and rewrite the database layer.
I already ordered hardware without asking.

items.explanation: Risk updates should include timeline, impact, options, recommendation, and a decision date.

items.scenario: You will miss a committed date because a dependency team delayed their API.
items.prompt: What should you tell your manager?

choices.text: It is not my fault.
We will miss Thursday's date because Payments API delivery slipped to next Monday. New ETA is next Wednesday. I have a workaround spike in progress and will confirm feasibility by tomorrow noon.
Maybe we can still make it somehow.
I did not want to bother you with this.

items.explanation: Bad news early, with cause, new ETA, and mitigation — no blame theater.

items.scenario: Your manager asks whether the team can take on an urgent partner integration this quarter.
items.prompt: What is a clear capacity response?

choices.text: Sure, we can do everything.
We can take it if we pause the observability upgrade or add one contractor. Without that tradeoff, quality risk is high. Which priority should we protect?
No. Never.
Let me think and never follow up.

items.explanation: Good capacity answers offer tradeoffs and ask for a priority decision.

items.scenario: You need approval to buy a monitoring tool that costs $18k/year. ROI is reduced MTTR and fewer pages for the on-call team.

choices.text: Please approve this tool because other companies use it.
Requesting approval for $18k/year monitoring. Expected outcome: cut median MTTR by ~25% and reduce noisy pages. Pilot for 30 days with success metrics attached. Can we decide this week?
I already signed up for the annual plan.
If we do not buy this, the team will quit.

items.explanation: Budget asks need cost, expected outcome, measurement, and a decision timeline.

items.scenario: After a SEV-1, your manager wants a same-day summary for the VP.

choices.text: We had a bad day with Kubernetes and Redis and DNS and deploys.

Summary for VP: 47 minutes of checkout degradation. Root cause: bad feature flag default. Mitigated by disabling flag. Customer impact: ~9% failed checkouts. Follow-ups: flag defaults review and canary checks — owners assigned, due Friday.
Please read the raw Slack thread.
Someone made a mistake; details TBD.

items.explanation: Exec summaries: duration, impact, cause at right altitude, mitigation, and dated follow-ups.

items.scenario: Your 1:1 is starting. You want to discuss feeling overloaded by interrupt-driven work.
items.prompt: How do you raise it productively?

choices.text: I am drowning and this job is impossible.
I want to discuss interrupt load. This week I spent about 60% of time on ad-hoc requests, which delayed the auth migration. Can we define an intake path and protect two focus blocks daily?
I will just work nights to catch up.
Everyone else has it easier than I do.

items.explanation: Use data, impact on commitments, and a concrete process ask.

items.scenario: A project is green on delivery but red on quality (flaky tests rising). Your manager only asked about dates.

choices.text: Dates are fine, nothing else matters.
Delivery date is still green, but quality risk is rising: flaky tests up 30% this month. I propose a two-day stabilization window before the release; otherwise we accept higher rollback risk.
QA will somehow handle it.
I prefer not to mention problems.

items.explanation: Surface hidden risk with a recommended tradeoff even when not asked.

items.scenario: You disagree with a leadership directive to skip canaries for a hot fix.

choices.text: That is reckless and I will not do it.
I understand the urgency. Skipping canaries increases blast radius. I recommend a 5-minute canary on 5% traffic with auto-rollback. If we must go faster, please confirm we accept the elevated risk.
Whatever you say.
I will complain in a side channel after the meeting.

items.explanation: Disagree by acknowledging goal, stating risk, offering a safer alternative, and clarifying decision ownership.

items.scenario: End of day. Your manager is offline. You need to leave an async update about a production change.

choices.text: Did a thing in prod.

Shipped rate-limit change to production at 17:40 local. Expected: fewer abuse spikes. Watch: 429 rate and checkout success. Rollback command documented in the change ticket. Ping me if 429s exceed 2% for 10 minutes.
Please review all dashboards when you are back.
No update; talk tomorrow.

items.explanation: Async updates need what changed, expected effect, what to watch, and rollback cues.
